Submission Instructions

Scope — one page of one document. Your project describes a single page of a single document: one sheet, leaf, fragment, or printed face, described completely. Do not work across several items.

What “one page” means for your object, since the phrase comes from codicology and fits a bound manuscript better than the rest: for a codex it is one complete recto or verso; for a loose sheet, scrap, or broadside it is that one complete sheet; for a printed decree it is one page of the impression. If your object is torn or fragmentary, say so, and state in a sentence why it still counts as a describable whole. If it does not, choose another page — there is no penalty for switching early, and a fragment that cannot be described completely will cost you later.

  1. Establish what your object actually is. Record the holding institution, the shelfmark or reference number, and whether you are looking at the original, a contemporary copy, a later transcript, or a printed edition. If no original survives, say so and name the oldest extant exemplar — that is a finding, not a gap.
  2. Identify the authority files that govern your document, and justify them. Trismegistos, Pinakes, and Diktyon serve Greek literary manuscripts; they do not describe your three documents. Name the registries that do apply — see the Authority Control card in the workshop resources for starting points — and record at least two stable identifiers (ARK, call number, VIAF, or equivalent) with the exact syntax you found them in. If a standard authority file exists but has no record for your object, state that; a verified absence is a legitimate result.
  3. Write a valid TEI XML snippet containing <teiHeader> with full <msIdentifier>, <msContents>, and <physDesc>. Describe the physical object you have: support and material, extent, layout, script or type, hands or printers, seals, watermarks, and condition. Use only the categories that honestly apply. A printed broadside has no quires and no scribal hand; forcing empty elements to fill a template is worse than omitting them, and leaving a category out with a reason is the correct scholarly move.
  4. Prompt an LLM (e.g. Claude or GPT-4) to extract the same metadata from a raw catalogue entry or archival description of your document, and identify at least two subtle hallucinations or schema violations — errors that survive automatic validation. Confident, well-formed, schema-valid metadata that is simply false counts, and is the most important category to catch.
  5. Submit your validated TEI snippet and a 300–500 word comparison detailing where the machine beat you, where it lied to you, and what that implies for structured schemas as a defence against probabilistic error.

Note on the exercise. Your three documents are not Greek manuscripts, and the standard cataloguing vocabulary will not always fit them. Where you have to make a judgement call — about genre, about which element to use, about whether to describe something at all — write one sentence saying why. Those sentences are graded, and they are the part of this assignment that transfers to any future document you catalogue.
